news.title: President Trump wants 60-day pause to analyse global impact of sanctions and tariffs: Marco Rubio
news.text: UNITED STATES: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to "analyze" their impact on the global economy."The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis."These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices" but on economies as well, Rubio said.Trump said late Saturday his decision would benefit the US, though it was unclear if he had actually made up his mind on the matter."We'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," he said. "It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world."US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticized Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia -- measures adopted by Congress last month.The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas..Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold.The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine.But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions."Beyond irresponsible," Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X."If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move "a mistake" in comments aired on Fox News.Trump's executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.Polls show Trump's Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls."The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump's action "rewards" Putin..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Trump says Iran war will end ‘very quickly’, predicts lower US gas prices
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday (local time) expressed confidence that the ongoing war with Iran would end “very quickly”, claiming that the conclusion of hostilities would bring down energy costs for American consumers.

Addressing a crowd of supporters during a campaign rally in Kentucky, Trump linked the outcome of the Middle East conflict directly to domestic gas prices, promising that fuel costs would plummet once operations conclude.

“It’s going to end very quickly. When it ends, your gas prices are going to be lower than what they were before,” Trump said.

During his speech, the President revisited previous military strikes against Iranian targets, framing the operations as a necessary preemptive action to neutralise Tehran’s nuclear ambitions.

Trump defended the decisions made during what he described as an “excursion,” asserting that the strikes successfully crippled Iran’s nuclear development capabilities.

“You know, when I did the little excursion to the Islamic, the beautiful Islamic Republic of Iran, we beat the shit out of them. But when I did that excursion, we knocked out their nuclear capacity,” Trump told the rally.

Trump defends strikes to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons

Addressing lingering debates over the strategic cost of the strikes, Trump insisted that preventing a nuclear-armed Iran was the paramount priority for national security.

“Somebody said, ‘Oh, well, was it worth it?’ I said, ‘They cannot have a nuclear weapon; they can’t, because they’ll use it,’” Trump added.

Iran calls for end to hostilities across all fronts

Meanwhile, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh stressed that ending hostilities across all fronts was essential to achieving lasting peace in the region, warning that continued fighting in any area would prolong the wider conflict.

According to the state-run IRNA news agency, citing Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network, Khatibzadeh said Iran remained committed to ending the Israeli war on Lebanon and had secured this objective in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which Iran and the United States signed in mid-June this year. He said Lebanon was among the key issues discussed between Iran and the US, adding that he sought to bring the two sides closer during his visit to Beirut.

The senior Iranian official, who reached the Lebanese capital on Wednesday for talks with local leaders, described the exchanges as “good” and confirmed meetings with Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Foreign Ministry representatives. He insisted that Israel must stop its war in Lebanon and the Levant, pointing out that events in the two areas remain closely linked.

Tehran accuses US and Israel of violating memorandum

Khatibzadeh also charged that Washington and Tel Aviv had breached the Islamabad memorandum of understanding by launching strikes on Iran and Lebanon. He observed that American attempts to arrange a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had stalled, declaring that Israel could not be relied upon to keep its word and that the United States bore responsibility for reining in its ally.

Labelling the US war on Iran unlawful under international law, the deputy foreign minister said Washington had been unable to eliminate Iran’s air defences or its ability to deter attacks. Tehran, he added, had withstood an existential war and would continue safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Iran says it is ready to address nuclear concerns

Iran stood prepared to respond to questions raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency and the United States concerning its peaceful nuclear programme, he stated, referring to more than 15 IAEA reports that verified Iranian compliance. Tehran had further offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, stressing that it did not pursue war but would counter any imposed conflict.

Published on October 18, 2026
news.summary: The contrasting statements come as Washington defends its military campaign and Tehran demands an end to fighting across the region

news.title: Newsom Breaks Silence on Ex-Wife Guilfoyle’s Greek Tragedy
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom was pressed to weigh in on the plight of his now-disgraced ex, Kimberly Guilfoyle, on Saturday.

Newsom is a vocal critic and frequent online troll of President Donald Trump and his administration, but he has stayed silent on the mounting scandal surrounding Guilfoyle.

That changed while he was campaigning for Democratic candidates in New Hampshire ahead of the midterms, when a CBS reporter put him on the spot. 

“Recently, your ex-wife Kimberly Guilfoyle was involved in a scandal and pushed out of her ambassadorship. Could you please share what your reaction was to that news?” Jared Ochacher of CBS News asked Newsom, leaving him little room to dodge the dreaded conversation.

Newsom appeared less than enthusiastic about the question, rubbing his eyes before responding.

“I don’t know enough about it,” he said. “I haven’t talked to her in a while. I just wish her the best, and I don’t have much, honestly, much more to say on it. It’s unfortunate.”

Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Newsom and Guilfoyle were introduced at a political event in 1994 and began dating shortly afterward. The couple married in December 2001 and filed for divorce in January 2005, just over three years later. They finalized their divorce in February 2006. 

Guilfoyle was romantically linked to Donald Trump Jr. from 2018 until 2024, and the pair were engaged from 2020 until they split after rumors began to circulate that Don Jr. was spending time with Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson that summer. 

Anderson and Don Jr. married on May 21, celebrating with a lavish three-day party in the Bahamas reportedly bankrolled by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin. 

The president, who did not attend the wedding, later claimed his son had reimbursed Kremlev for the festivities.

Guilfoyle reportedly remained in the president’s good graces after the couple’s split, and she was appointed U.S. ambassador to Greece.

But it all came crumbling down when a Republican donor released texts he claimed were between him and Guilfoyle, in which she allegedly asked him to pay her $100,000 American Express bill in exchange for access to the Trumps.

Guilfoyle denied the claims and said the texts were doctored. The donor, former Kentucky congressional candidate Eric Deters, has not backed down.

The scandal only got worse, with more allegations of cash for access surfacing. 

Then-White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia announced Guilfoyle’s firing on live TV on Tuesday, during her first—and only—press conference. Zacharia herself got the ax after five days on the job.

Newsom is a vocal critic and frequent online troll of President Donald Trump and his administration, but he has stayed silent on the mounting scandal surrounding Guilfoyle.

news.title: Zelenskyy terms restricting military use of Starlink in Ukraine deliberate
news.text: Restrictions on Ukraine’s military use of SpaceX’s Starshield, a militarised version of Starlink, appear to be deliberate and not the result of any technical problems, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.Speed limitations on the internet network remain in place across Ukraine, resulting in a significant slowing down of connections, Zelenskyy said in audio messages to reporters on WhatsApp. Ukraine sent vehicles connected to Starshield to Europe to conduct speed checks and found they operated normally, Zelenskyy said. The restrictions “are on the territory of Ukraine –– so it is a planned operation,” he said.US President Donald Trump said Friday that he didn’t order any limitations on Ukraine’s access to the system and didn’t think SpaceX Chairman Elon Musk had either. Musk on Wednesday said “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately” the president. news.title: Trump blocking Russia curbs historic moment: Putin envoy
news.text: US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive a new package of sanctions on Russia is a “historic moment”, a Russian presidential envoy said Saturday. Trump signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.The move came amid a clash with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that has fuelled speculation the US leader is increasingly siding with Moscow nearly five years into Russia’s offensive against Ukraine, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment,” Kirill Dmitriev, envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media.The Kremlin and Putin –– who appeared in military uniform Friday and said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine –– have not yet reacted to the move, which is a major diplomatic win for Russia. The Lindsey Graham Act –– named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill –– targeted Russia’s energy and defence sectors as well as Putin and other senior officials.Dmitriev said the act would have caused “serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets”. The West imposed massive sanctions on Russia when it launched the Ukraine war in 2022.Russia on Saturday carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian infrastructure targets including the country’s largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The plant is owned by steel giant ArcelorMittal, which suspended operations there in Sept after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.In a statement, Russia’s defence ministry said the plant supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.It said Russian forces had also hit an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line.A cargo vessel in the Black Sea was also hit, the ministry said, alleging that it was delivering military cargo to Odesa. news.title: ‘Standing up for democracy’: Atlanta ‘No Kings’ rally draws Trump critics ahead of midterms
news.text:
Standing behind a big, blue “Defending Democracy” sign, Kelsea Bond addressed a gathering at a park in midtown Atlanta on Saturday at the start of a “No Kings” rally, one of many across the US, as the country prepares to go to the polls in the November 3 midterm elections.

“We need to build a society that works for the working class, not the billionaires,” said Bond.

“Yeah!” many in the crowd responded. “Right!” added a woman holding a “In 2026: Dump Trump” placard. 

“We need an economy, we need a society that is democratically run by working people because we keep this economy running,” said Bond, a labour organiser, politician and elected member of the Atlanta City Council.

At 33, Bond is the youngest serving councillor and its first Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member. A political group championing progressive issues, the DSA is not a political party. Bond ran for the District 2 seat on the city council last year as an independent candidate.

DSA members are focused on getting the Democrats to address progressive issues, sparking headlines on differences between mainstream and left-wing camps within the party.

Read moreOssoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party

But with a little over two weeks to go before election day, Bond is focused on issues that unite President Donald Trump’s critics.

“I’m here because we’re standing up for democracy in Georgia today,” Bond told FRANCE 24 in an interview as a few shoppers at a farmer’s market in another corner of the park strolled over to join the demonstration. “The Republicans, who have been in-charge for several decades in Georgia, have done a lot to roll back voting rights and attack the right to vote here in this state. Earlier in the summer, they were threatening to redraw our maps to favour Republicans. So, voting rights have very much been under attack in the state of Georgia.”

Some US states have redrawn congressional districts this year after an April 29 Supreme Court ruling enabled mid-cycle redistricting to give a political advantage to a particular party. These include a number of Republican “red” southern states in the US. In June, Georgia’s Republican state legislative leaders rejected a redistricting bid ahead of the November midterms for fear of a voter backlash against the party. But many Democrats fear the state’s Republican politicians will attempt to put the issue back on the agenda after the midterms.

“No Kings” protests erupted across the US after Trump, in February 2025, posted an AI-generated image of himself as a monarch on a fake "Time" magazine cover. A number of these anti-Trump protests have drawn large gatherings in major US cities. But the purpose of Saturday’s mobilisation was more targeted, according to organisers.

“The intention behind this is more of a community engagement, to get people excited about the midterm elections. The aim is to encourage people to not only get out and vote – hopefully vote early – but to also get to know their neighbours and take their neighbours with them to polling locations,” said Kimberly Diemert, communications director for 50501 Georgia, one of many community groups that worked together to organise the rally.

“By breaking up the larger mass events into smaller events, we're able to gather people at a community location and walk them to a polling place,” Diemert added.

ICE on the agenda

At the Atlanta rally, the gathering of around 300 people marched roughly a mile from the historic Piedmont Park down to St. Mark’s, a local church. The city’s police force secured the route, holding back traffic as protesters followed a lively street band at the head of the rally belting out rousing tunes.

The atmosphere was defiant, but not menacing, with the crowd including grannies and toddlers in strollers. Protesters carried signs denouncing many of Trump’s policies – at times in profane terms.

“There are so many transgressions and terrible things that this administration is doing on a daily basis. But ICE is possibly the most evil and disgusting of all,” said 37-year-old Daniel, holding a “Fuck Ice” sign.

The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency was a frequently cited target of ire at Saturday’s rally.

“I'm really tired of what's going on in America. And when I see people being rounded up by ICE, immigrants who have been here for a long time, it just makes me really, really sad. I want change,” said Piper White.

A war ‘with no end in sight’

Trump’s foreign policies also came under attack, with one banner, shaped like a Russian doll, featuring a caricature of Trump. The cardboard cut-out split at the belly with a lever to reveal a sinister photograph of Russian President Vladimir Putin lurking inside Trump’s tummy. 

“It’s Donald Trump and Putin in a matryoshka doll thing – showing that they’re working together. If I had room I would have put another in there, like Elon Musk maybe,” said Marilyn, who declined to provide her surname. “Foreign policy is one of the most important issues in this election. I’m completely against the war in Iran and I support Ukraine,” she explained.

Mark Spivey said he was “disgusted” with Trump’s war in Iran. “All the taxpayer money that we contribute to the system, you're taking it to get into a foreign war,” he said. “Prices are higher. Inflation is higher. We're in a war – an endless war. It was supposed to last a couple of weeks, three weeks, four weeks, six weeks. We're over eight months into this war now, and there's no end in sight.”

By lunchtime, the rally had reached St. Mark’s church, where organisers asked protesters if they would like to volunteer as election observers. For those who replied in the affirmative, a workshop on election protection and observation was held inside the church.

“We just want to make sure that this is a free and fair election where everyone's vote counts,” said Trish Murphy from Necessary Action Georgia, a grassroots political action group based in Atlanta. “In the past, there have been accusations that some elections were not fair. But they were,” she noted, referring to, but not explicitly citing, Trump’s allegations that he won the 2020 vote against Joe Biden. “So, this time, we want to make sure that everyone observes, and to make sure that there is no election interference.”
news.summary: “No Kings, Vote Now” was the theme of a rally in Atlanta, one of many organised across the US on Saturday. While many demonstrators denounced President Donald Trump’s policies, organisers said the rally was aimed at getting out the vote in the November 3 midterm elections and protecting democracy in America.
news.author: Leela Jacinto

Rubio was responding to questions on Saturday evening ahead of his departure for a week-long tour of Uzbekistan and India.

news.title: Trump waives key sanctions against Russia
news.text:
Issues waiver days before penalties due; executive order cites national interests
• Zelensky says move ‘emboldens’ Putin; Kremlin envoy hails ‘historic moment’

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump on Saturday waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs days before they were due to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.

Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September. The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, which began in 2022, but it lets the president waive sanctions simply by informing Congress that they are not in the national interest.

The executive order, released by the White House on Friday, said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate”.

“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump said in the order.

The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100 per cent within 30 days on all goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought Russian oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a message on X on Saturday that the move emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin, all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground,” wrote Zelensky, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday.

Trump has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticising Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.

Weeks before US midterm elections, in which Trump’s Repu-blicans are battling to keep their narrow grip on Congress, the measures could have raised oil prices as Americans face higher costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.

China and India, among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, had raised concerns about the bill. Beijing said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law”, while India warned Washington that new tariffs could affect bilateral ties.

US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, criticised the waiver. “Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s investment envoy, called the waiver “a truly historic moment” in a post on X.

news.title: Trump Makes $100 Million Promise to Kentucky if GOP Wins Midterms
news.text: President Donald Trump promised a $100 million investment in pharmaceutical manufacturing in Kentucky on Saturday but appeared to condition the funding on Republicans winning November's midterm elections. “If the Republicans win, the Department of War will be investing $100 million in the pharmaceutical company Antheia to revitalize [a] gigantic drug manufacturing facility in Winchester, Kentucky,” Trump said during a rally in Highland Heights. “That's a big one.” Trump spoke at Truist Arena on Northern Kentucky University's campus as part of a midterm campaign push for Republicans ahead of the November 3 election. Kentucky Republicans expected at the event included Republican Senate candidate Andy Barr and 4th Congressional District candidate Ed Gallrein. Gallrein defeated incumbent Republican Representative Thomas Massie in this year's GOP primary after receiving Trump's backing. The president's wording appeared to explicitly tie the $100 million investment to the outcome of the midterms. Details about how the proposed investment would be structured, when it would be made, and the precise status of the Winchester facility were not immediately clear. Newsweek has reached out to Antheia for comment and further details about the proposed investment. The announcement came as Trump made manufacturing and the economy central themes of his speech. He predicted economic improvements as new plants come online. “Those plants are going to be opening in a year, and when they open you're going to see numbers that nobody's ever seen before,” Trump said. What Does Antheia Make? Antheia, a California-based pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturer, produces key starting materials, or KSMs, and active pharmaceutical ingredients, or APIs, used in essential medicines. The company says its biosynthesis technology offers an alternative to pharmaceutical supply chains dependent on agricultural sources, which can be vulnerable to poor yields and other disruptions. The company's first commercial product is thebaine, a starting material used to manufacture medication for severe and postsurgical pain, overdose reversal, and addiction treatment. Antheia announced its first commercial delivery of thebaine in 2024 and has also been developing ingredients including oripavine and scopolamine. Trump's announcement comes amid a broader federal push to increase domestic production of critical pharmaceutical ingredients. In March, the Department of Health and Human Services' (HHS) Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response announced a $9 million award to Antheia to expand domestic production of thebaine. The agency said the ingredient is used to manufacture medicines for pain management, alcohol use disorder, and opioid overdose reversal, while citing reliance on foreign supply chains as a potential vulnerability. Antheia had previously received another government-backed project agreement valued at up to $12 million through a program funded by HHS' Defense Production Act Title III program. The $100 million figure Trump announced Saturday would therefore be considerably larger than either of those previously announced federal commitments, although details about the proposed Winchester project and what would be manufactured there have not yet been established publicly. Trump Addresses Iran, Protesters at Kentucky Rally Trump also addressed the ongoing conflict with Iran during Saturday's rally, saying: “It's going to end very quickly.” At another point, he called the U.S. action against Iran an “excursion,” saying: “When I did the little excursion to the beautiful Islamic Republic of Iran, we beat the s*** out of 'em.” The rally was briefly interrupted by a protester who was removed by security. Trump accused the person of being a paid protester, saying such demonstrators receive $250, before weighing whether the person should face charges. “We shouldn't ruin his life and press charges, right? Just let him go,” Trump said before responding to people in the crowd: “Oh, no? Let's think about it.” Trump was distracted later by another person in the arena and asked whether the individual was a “friend or foe.” “I think he's a friend. Are you friend or foe?” Trump asked. “Because being a foe in this arena can be a very dangerous thing.” The protester episodes came during a wide-ranging speech in which Trump also discussed Venezuela, saying: “You know how much money we're taking out of Venezuela? Hundreds of billions of dollars we're taking out of Venezuela.” What Are the Most Competitive Kentucky Races? Trump's visit comes as Kentucky voters prepare to choose a successor to longtime Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, who is not seeking another term. Barr is running against Democrat Charles Booker for the open Senate seat. Public polling in the race has been limited. A Global Strategy Group poll released by Booker's campaign found Barr leading Booker 49 percent to 40 percent among 600 likely Kentucky voters. The survey was conducted August 24 to 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. A closer battle is unfolding in Kentucky's open 6th Congressional District, which Barr is vacating to run for Senate. Republican Ralph Alvarado faces Democrat Zach Dembo for the seat. A Change Research poll conducted online from September 29 to October 5 for Kentuckians Not Corruption, which is affiliated with Dembo, according to the New York Times, found Dembo leading Alvarado 47 percent to 38 percent, with 8 percent undecided. The survey included 524 likely voters in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Trump held Saturday's rally in the 4th Congressional District, where Republican Ed Gallrein faces Democrat Melissa Strange. Recent public polling of that general-election matchup was not available. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Trump tied a $100 million investment in Kentucky pharmaceutical manufacturing to Republicans winning the midterm elections.

news.title: ‘No Kings’ protesters spurn organizers' rules: ‘This is as partisan as you can get’
news.text: ALEXANDRIA, Va. — On South Washington Street, 26-year-old environmental engineer Nayely Cruz Hernandez had a straightforward message for voters as she joined a phalanx of protesters lining the street for nationwide "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump: "Vote blue." "We got to take the power away from Trump, from the Republicans," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. "So we got to win the House, we got to win the Senate, not only in Virginia, but across the country." Standing beside her boyfriend, Noah Schwarzott, 25, their 13-year-old Maltese-poodle, Maybellene, in her arms, Hernandez acknowledged that national No Kings organizers had their own rules for the protests to be "nonpartisan," but she wasn't following orders. 'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS "The No King ... organizers can say whatever," she said. "But I'm saying vote blue, because why are we here? news.title: Trump vows ‘very good decision’ on anti-Russian sanctions
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 18. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has stated that he intends to make a "very good decision" regarding anti-Russian sanctions, one that will benefit the entire world.

"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out. It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world because we're really at a world stage," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, according to the White House press pool.

Earlier on Saturday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that Trump set a 60-day window to evaluate the potential consequences of imposing sanctions on Russia, as well as the associated tariffs on other nations, including the impact on both the U.S. and global economies. According to Rubio, this additional analysis is prompted by the current volatility in global energy markets.

Previously, Trump signed an executive order suspending the application of the anti-Russian measures stipulated by the new law, pending further instructions from the president or the secretary of state. On September 18, Trump signed a bill passed by Congress that mandates tougher sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership, as well as state-owned enterprises. The legislation includes provisions for a 500% increase in tariffs on imports from Russia, and a 100% increase on imports from countries that are major purchasers of Russian energy. Under the terms of the law, the U.S. administration may opt not to implement these measures if it deems them contrary to the national interests of the United States.
news.summary: According to the US president, the decision will benefit the entire world

news.title: Trump takes 60 days to assess impact of potential sanctions against Russia — Rubio
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 18. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump intends to use a 60-day window to evaluate how potential sanctions against Russia and related tariffs on other nations could affect the US and global economies, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters.

"The problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries, India, for example, and others. And so, I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.

The secretary of state noted that the additional analysis is prompted by tensions in global energy markets. He highlighted that energy supplies are facing pressures from the situation involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and strikes on energy infrastructure during the Russia-Ukraine conflict, all of which drive global energy prices.

Rubio also pointed to India, which, he said, is "voluntarily diversifying their energy portfolio" but still imports "substantial amount of energy from Russia because it is hard to pivot everything from one day to the next."

"But they [India] are also an important ally and partner of the United States," he remarked, emphasizing that Washington must weigh these factors to find the optimal mix of sanctions and tariffs.
news.summary: The US secretary of state noted that the additional analysis is prompted by tensions in global energy markets

news.title: Meta says suspending No Kings account on day of action was done 'in error'
news.text: Meta said Saturday that an automatic trigger is to blame for the No Kings movement's Instagram account being suspended in the midst of a nationwide effort to mobilize early voting in the midterms. The network, which bills itself as nonpartisan but arose last year in response to President Donald Trump's actions, said its account went dark for "several hours" at the peak of its event. "Even after visibility was restored, we had no access to the account for hours," the group posted on its account. In a statement on X, Meta spokesman Andy Stone said that accounts posting, sharing, or commenting at "very high frequencies" can prompt an automated response. "That's what happened with the No Kings IG account in the lead up to today's day of action. Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error," he said in an X post. "Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologize." No Kings said it wants a deeper explanation from Meta. "Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable," it said in its post. "Meta must answer for this suspension and take immediate steps to ensure it never happens again — to any account, but especially those working to inform voters and encourage participation in our democracy." The group said it held nearly 3,000 rallies across the country to encourage voters to cast their ballots early as a hedge against any effort to undermine turnout in an election that will determine the balance of power in Congress.
news.summary: Meta blamed an automatic trigger for the suspension that made the No Kings account go dark.

news.title: US ambassador urges Israel to prosecute attackers of American journalist  - Dominican Republic Post –
news.text:
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank.

“Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday.

“Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”

Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual harvest of olives on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians.

Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses.

The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said.

Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera that Levine “was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground.”

Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah.

The American photojournalist underwent surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, and was left with a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations, her daughter told The Associated Press news agency.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of closely fought October 27 elections, claimed on Friday that Palestinians or “far-left” activists may have been responsible for the attack on Levine and other Palestinians.

Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has sharply criticised Israeli settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers after Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity.

The ambassador, appointed by US President Donald Trump, met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”.

The US State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.

news.title: Katie Zacharia's dramatic final moments as Trump's press secretary revealed
news.text:
The extraordinary circumstances surrounding Katie Zacharia's sudden departure as Donald Trump's White House press secretary have been revealed, including the moment she was summoned away from an interview and never returned.

The 42-year-old had been in the prestigious role for just five days when her brief tenure came to an abrupt end on Friday, October 16 2026.

According to a new report by The Wall Street Journal, Katie was sitting behind her desk in the West Wing, discussing her plans for the future with reporters, when a senior adviser to the president knocked on her office door.

Jason Miller entered the room and delivered an unexpected message, telling her: "JD wanted to chat with us real quick."

The comment was a reference to Vice President JD Vance, who apparently wanted to speak to the pair.

Katie promptly left the interview to attend the meeting, but never returned. Shortly afterwards, news emerged that she had been removed from her position.

The precise details of her conversation with JD have not been disclosed, although the unexpected summons marked the end of her remarkably short stint in the role.

Just moments before being summoned away, Katie had confidently outlined her plans for the White House press team, insisting that no staffing changes were on the horizon.

"There are no staffing changes that are happening," she reportedly told the WSJ, adding that she wanted to keep the team working together.

Around the same time, Donald Trump was speaking to reporters outside the White House, where he revealed that he had already advised Katie to reconsider her position.

"I said, 'Is this for you Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this,'" the president explained. "Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider."

The President went on to suggest that the intense scrutiny surrounding Katie's appointment had taken its toll, expressing concern for the impact on her family.

President Trump, who had personally selected her for the role just a week earlier, insisted he wanted her to be happy rather than endure constant criticism.

Katie's departure followed several challenging days in the spotlight after she replaced former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

Her first and only White House press briefing on Tuesday lasted approximately 15 minutes, during which she relied heavily on prepared notes and answered questions from just three media outlets.

The performance attracted widespread criticism, with questions subsequently emerging about her legal qualifications.

Although Katie had previously described herself as a lawyer, she confirmed that she had failed the California bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine Law School in 2011.

She defended her professional background, explaining that she had worked in international transaction law in China but had never been licensed to practise law in the United States.

In a statement previously supplied to HELLO!, Katie said: "I practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

Katie later told The Wall Street Journal that she had been given less than 24 hours to prepare for her first press briefing and received essential background materials only that morning.

Despite the difficult circumstances, she maintained that she had tried her best and did not blame the White House for asking her to take on the assignment at such short notice.

Following her departure, Katie took to social media to publicly thank her former boss, making it clear that she continued to hold the President in high regard.

"President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man," she wrote alongside a photograph of the pair in the Oval Office.

"I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him."
news.summary: The mother-of-four was interrupted during an interview at the White House and never returned, bringing her five-day tenure to an abrupt end

news.title: Relief for India as Trump waives sanctions related to Russian fuel purchase under Lindsey Graham Act
news.text:
Washington DC [US], October 17 (ANI): US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, a month after signing the Bill. 

The law, which has now been paused, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% on goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas which includes India and China. 

The move comes amid a diesel deal with Russia in the backdrop of soaring diesel prices in the United States ahead of the November midterm elections.

Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorises the President to waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty under the law.

'I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act,' Trump said in the order.

He waived the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Act, which allowed Trump to increase the rate of duty on all goods imported into the United States from Russia to a rate of up to 500 per cent ad valorem (relative to the value). It also allowed a duty up to 100 per cent ad valorem from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas.

This comes after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, under which he said Russia would immediately supply more than 3,00,000 tonnes of diesel fuel, followed by another 5,00,000 tonnes during November and 1 million tonnes immediately thereafter.

In a Truth Social post, he said a further 3 million tonnes would follow within a short period, depending on the condition of Russia's diesel refineries.

Trump has hailed the diesel deal with Russia as a 'big deal', thanking Putin for agreeing to supply 'massive amounts' of diesel to the United States.

India had expressed concerns to Washington over the 'Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026' amid a lurking threat of tariff imposition.

On Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs reiterated India's stance on global market stability amid the US-Russia diesel deal.

'As far as the diesel deal is concerned, we do not wish to comment on commercial arrangements that have been made between two countries, except to say that we have always advocated for stability in global energy markets,' Randhir Jaiswal stated.

At the same time, Jaiswal noted that India has directly raised its objections regarding American legal measures targeting Russian trade ties, specifically the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA).

'We have already conveyed to the US side our concerns regarding the SRIA legislation,' he said. (ANI)

news.title: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure
news.text:
New Delhi [India], October 17 (ANI): US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy.

Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.

The order provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18, but suspends their application through a presidential waiver.

'Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order,' the White House Executive Order stated.

The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn, while existing Russia-related sanctions under other Executive Orders remain unaffected.

According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), the decision provides India temporary relief but leaves open the possibility of Washington restoring tariff pressure during future trade negotiations.

In its report titled 'U.S. Waives Russian-Oil Tariffs: Temporary Relief for India, but Uncertainty Remains,' GTRI said, 'For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty.'

R Ramachandran, former Director (Refineries) at Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), told ANI that the immediate benefit for Indian oil companies would be greater crude sourcing flexibility rather than necessarily higher refining margins.

'So more than the GRM, what actually impact it will have on Indian refineries will be the availability of more crude choices,' he said.

Gross refining margin (GRM) refers to the difference between the value of petroleum products produced by a refinery and the cost of crude oil processed.

Ramachandran explained that increased Russian crude availability could help refiners secure more economical supplies, depending on discounts. However, lower crude prices could also be accompanied by falling petroleum product prices, limiting gains in refining margins.

Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, said Russia's importance to India has increasingly shifted from discounted oil towards ensuring uninterrupted supplies.

'The discount has really reduced significantly. But yes, what is more important for India now is availability and ensuring consistent supply of crude oil for the economy,' Sinha told ANI.

She said Russia's share of India's crude imports had exceeded 30 per cent in recent years, although its price advantage over international benchmarks had narrowed.

GTRI noted that Russia's share in India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as purchases shifted towards the United States and the United Arab Emirates.

The think tank also highlighted Washington's own energy requirements as a possible factor behind the waiver.

According to its report, the United States agreed to purchase Russian diesel under an October 9 agreement to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices.

It also noted that Washington had agreed not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that targeting India alone could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations.

'The message is clear: U.S. interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection,' GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said in the report.

Meanwhile, Ramachandran said a sustained waiver could help reduce freight costs and ease logistical constraints associated with Russian oil shipments.

He said greater vessel availability and smoother payment arrangements could improve crude procurement economics.

'If Russia and India can agree upon on a continued ruble-rupee exchange for this, it also supports to ease the foreign exchange outgo which currently is affecting the Indian Rupee's strength,' he said.

However, these benefits would depend on the restrictions that remain applicable.

On the broader economic impact, Sinha said India's current account deficit could remain manageable despite elevated crude prices, supported by merchandise and services exports.

She expects the current account deficit to remain between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent of GDP, assuming crude prices range between USD 80 and USD 100 per barrel during the remaining financial year.

However, persistently higher prices could widen the deficit towards 1.5 per cent of GDP under adverse conditions.

Sinha expects average inflation of around 5 to 5.5 per cent, although higher fuel costs and food inflation remain risks.

She said the fiscal impact would depend on whether elevated oil costs are absorbed through excise duty reductions, oil marketing companies or higher retail fuel prices.

Healthy tax collections and potential disinvestment receipts, including from IDBI Bank, could help the government manage fiscal pressures, she added.

On the rupee, Sinha said the waiver could improve market sentiment but was unlikely to provide substantial direct support to the currency.

She also stressed that a lasting India-US trade agreement would offer greater economic stability than temporary tariff relief, warning that fresh US tariff threats could emerge.

Ramachandran cautioned against immediately entering long-term Russian crude supply agreements without clarity on the waiver's duration.

'The first thing I would say is that it is too early to look at jumping into long-term contracts,' he said.

He added that refiners would need to assess whether Russian crude discounts and stable supply conditions could be sustained.

GTRI similarly warned India against making permanent trade concessions in exchange for temporary relief.

'India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed U.S. pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions,' Srivastava said. (ANI)

news.title: White House AI Task Force Adopts Charter, Starts 120-Day Clock
news.text:
The White House’s artificial intelligence task force adopted its charter Thursday, opening a 120-day window to advise on how much of an oversight role Washington should take.

The panel agreed after its first official meeting to commission a report from the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology evaluating AI risk, according to Semafor. The review covers cybersecurity and critical-infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability.

A White House official said the group would reach outside government as it carries out its mandate.

Throughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts.

The task force also created a working group to implement the White House Accord on Super Intelligence that major AI chief executives signed this month, a process led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the task force’s chair, alongside National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.

Defense Undersecretary Emil Michael, a vice chair, will develop protocols for labs to report breaches, hacks, and other cyber incidents to the government. The Pentagon official will also interface with frontier labs on long-term coordination across the government.

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson will lead a law-enforcement and consumer-protection committee that includes the Justice Department, while Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor will handle critical-infrastructure protection and study AI’s impact on the American workforce with the Labor Department.

Members include Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, along with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters.

A White House official told Semafor that one potential lever is export controls, which the Commerce Department temporarily imposed on Anthropic after the company declined to grant the government unfettered access to its models.

The task force’s work follows President Donald Trump’s September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to replace “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence,” signed the same day roughly two dozen technology executives attended a White House luncheon and six frontier firms signed the voluntary Accord that Trump called “morally binding.”

Clayton, a former SEC chairman confirmed as intelligence chief over the summer, told the Wall Street Journal the administration’s priority is keeping the United States ahead of China.

“The risk of not being first is high,” Clayton said.

The White House’s artificial intelligence task force adopted its charter Thursday, opening a 120-day window to advise on how much of an oversight role Washington should take.

news.title: IMFC chair says global economy resilient
news.text:
BANGKOK: The global economy is showing great resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of the International Monetary Fund’s steering committee said on Saturday, while divisions over Russia’s war against Ukraine sparked a walkout of delegates.

Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who heads the IMF’s steering committee, asked about the walkout by nearly half of delegates during remarks by Russia’s finance minister at a meeting on Saturday, said the important thing was that members ultimately agreed to the chair’s statement.

“We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters,” the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee told Reuters.

Al-Jadaan told a press conference that the global economy was demonstrating “remarkable resilience” in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard.

“The message from the IMFC members is clear: There is no room for complacency,” Al-Jadaan said in the final press conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok.

Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment.

He said IMFC members called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by spillovers from wars and high energy prices.

“International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions,” he said.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the meetings productive but said there was clearly heightened anxiety among members about increasing divergence.

Many lower income countries that were not part of the AI-value chain feared they were falling behind, she said.

“These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation,” she said.

The Development Committee, which groups the boards of both the World Bank and the IMF, touched on similar themes in its statement, underscoring the urgent need to end wars and conflicts to ensure sustainable growth and long-term stability.

“Our priority remains to promote macroeconomic and financial stability while enabling broad-based, private sector-led growth, and strengthening resilience through credible policies and international cooperation,” the committee’s chair, Swedish Finance Minister Elisabeth Svantesson, said.

Those comments came shortly after many IMFC delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel told a bank event on the sidelines of the meetings that nearly 50% of delegates took part in the walkout, sending a clear message to Russia.

“This is a very strong signal about solidarity and values. It would be the best for the world economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine would end,” Nagel said. “I was really proud so many left this plenary.”

Ukraine’s central bank chief, Andriy Pyshnyi, told Reuters he was surprised by the large number of finance officials who left the room, calling it a “deep and emotional moment.”

The Bank of England confirmed that Governor Andrew Bailey was among the delegates who joined the walkout, which comes ahead of Britain hosting the G20 next year.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who may be in the frame to take over as chair of the World Economic Forum, stayed in the room, two people in the meeting said.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the IMFC, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years since. There were deep divisions again this week as tensions flared between the US and Ukraine.

People in the meeting said those who left while Siluanov spoke included delegates from Britain, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, among others.

“The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe,” one European diplomat said. “We cannot normalize relations with Russia.”

Germany on Thursday warned against efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers, just over a month after the US hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.

US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne told Reuters the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G20, supported Russia’s presence.

“We think it’s really important if you’re going to solve a crisis, you need to have open dialogue and open conversation,” she told Reuters. “And you can’t have … dialogue, and you can’t have resolution to conflict if no one’s talking to one another.”

Ukraine’s finance minister participated virtually in the meetings, in order to focus on budget priorities at home.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking at a European Union summit on Friday, blasted US President Donald Trump’s recent diesel deal with Russia.

EU leaders have rallied around Zelenskiy after Trump again criticised Ukraine and called its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace.” Trump on Friday waived a new congressional requirement to impose harsh sanctions on Russia.

news.title: China’s exports blow past forecasts, imports accelerate
news.text:
BEIJING: China’s export growth topped forecasts in September, with robust overseas demand helping offset weak consumer spending and easing pressure on policymakers to deliver this year’s growth goal.

Resilience in goods exports has for a second year defied pressure from Western countries seeking more balanced trade with China, keeping factories humming and shoring up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment.

Exports in September soared 36.3 percent from a year earlier, outstripping August’s 25.0 percent rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5 percent growth, customs data showed on Wednesday. September’s growth was the fastest since February this year when exports expanded 39.6 percent.

Imports jumped 31.0 percent, compared with 28.2 percent growth in August and economists’ forecasts of a 24.5 percent gain.

China’s trade surplus reached USD938.11 billion in the first nine months of the year, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to surpass USD1 trillion in surplus sooner than last year unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely.

A deal with the European Union to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier this month, is likely to weigh on China’s booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline.

President Xi Jinping’s September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on USD30 billion worth of goods from each side.

With the global build-out of AI infrastructure showing little sign of slowing, analysts expect demand for Chinese-made technology products, including semiconductors, to remain robust. China’s factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery.

BEIJING: China’s producer prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September while consumer inflation edged up, as pricier oil and commodities lifted factory-gate costs even as weak domestic demand kept broader price pressures contained.

news.title: US import prices increase; post largest annual gain in more than four years
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US import prices increased more than expected in September, boosted by higher costs for energy products and a range of other goods, further evidence of rising inflation pressures as the Middle East conflict persists.

The report from the Labour Department on Friday followed data this week showing strong increases in consumer and producer prices last month, which left economists convinced that inflation was broadening beyond the energy sector. The drawn-out US-Israeli war with Iran has snarled supply chains, and is keeping oil prices elevated.

Economists have attributed rising inflation to President Donald Trump’s policies, including tariffs on imports and the Middle East conflict. A Reuters/Ipsos poll also showed about 78 percent of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for the rising cost of living. “Americans face an inflation threat literally on every front and everywhere they turn they have to reach in their pocketbooks and pay a little bit more for the same goods that were cheaper just a few months ago,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “There was no import goods inflation before Trump 2.0 economic policies started to roll out in January 2025, but this year it is everywhere.”

Import prices jumped 1.1 percent last month after rebounding by a downwardly revised 0.5 percent in August, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, increasing 0.8 percent after a previously reported 0.7 percent advance in August. In the 12 months through September, import prices rose 8.1 percent, the largest gain since July 2022, after increasing 6.7 percent in August. Despite inflation heating up in September, financial markets still expected the Federal Reserve to skip raising interest rates later this month and tighten monetary policy in December.

The US central bank in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75 percent-4.00 percent range. Imported fuel prices rebounded 4.8 percent last month after falling 0.2 percent in August. Food prices were unchanged after dropping 0.6 percent in August. Excluding food and fuels, import prices advanced 0.7 percent, matching the prior month’s increase. The so-called core import prices rose 6.2 percent in the 12 months through September.

Capital goods prices increased 0.9 percent after rising by the same margin in August, boosted by prices for computers, peripherals and semiconductors amid an investment boom. There was also a rise in the cost of imported industrial and service machinery, which more than offset a decline in the prices of scientific and medical machinery.

Prices for imported consumer goods, excluding automotives, increased 0.4 percent, driven by a 0.7 percent surge in the cost of long-lasting manufactured goods. The cost of imported automotive vehicles, parts and engines increased 0.3 percent. Prices of imports from China increased 0.7 percent, the most since December 2021. Prices gained 3.1 percent in the 12 months through September. There were also increases in the prices of imports from Japan, the European Union, Mexico and Canada.

The report also showed a 12.6 percent surge in import air passenger fares last month. The rise, which followed decreases in July and August, could impact economists’ estimates of the Personal Consumption Expenditures price indexes, the inflation measures tracked by the Federal Reserve for its 2 percent target.

Economists’ estimates for the increase in September’s core PCE price index currently range from 0.31 percent to 0.36 percent, which could round up to 0.4 percent. That would translate to a year-over-year rise of 3.1 percent. Core PCE inflation gained 0.2 percent in August and advanced 3.0 percent on a year-over-year basis.

news.title: India’s goods trade deficit widens
news.text:
NEW DELHI: India’s merchandise trade deficit widened to USD30.21 billion in September as the rise in imports outpaced that in exports, though a rise in outbound shipments and trade deals could narrow the balance over coming months.

The trade gap has widened as Asia’s third-largest economy grapples with a prolonged Iran war that has made energy costlier, hurt shipments to the Middle East and battered markets.

India raised interest rates earlier this month and announced a raft of measures to support the rupee. India’s trade deficit stood at USD26.86 billion in August.

Merchandise exports rose to USD44.40 billion in September from USD43.81 billion in the previous month, while imports increased to USD74.61 billion from USD70.67 billion. Export growth was broad-based, reflecting strength across sectors including petroleum products, meat, dairy, poultry, electronic goods, handicrafts, and engineering goods, Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal told reporters.

India is seeking to diversify its export markets, with a trade deal with New Zealand set to take effect next week and its pact with the UK already in force, while a broader agreement with the EU is moving towards implementation.

Agrawal said negotiations with the US were moving in the “right direction,” with legal work underway. “We anticipate concluding and signing the trade deal at the earliest possible time,” Agrawal said, adding that India was seeking preferential market access and greater tariff stability under the proposed agreement.

Ties with the US have been rocky this past year over issues including President Donald Trump’s repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers.

The US remained the top destination for Indian exports, with goods shipments rising to USD50.81 billion in April-September from USD45.82 billion a year earlier.

India’s services exports stood at USD36.35 billion in September, and imports at USD19.44 billion, trade ministry estimates showed. Overall goods and services exports rose 13.84 percent year-on-year to USD476.20 billion in April-September from a year earlier, while imports increased 15.68 percent to USD551.13 billion, data showed.

news.title: Japan to invest up to USD21bn in two US chip factories to be run by GlobalFoundries
news.text:
NEW YORK: Japan will invest up to USD21 billion in two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries, the company said on Wednesday.

The move is part of a deal for Japan to invest USD550 billion in the US struck by President Donald Trump’s administration last year in return for the US lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25 percent to 15 percent.

The US will take a stake in the new chip factories, but Japan will provide all of the investment capital, GlobalFoundries said. The company, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Co, will earn fees from building and operating the factories, as well as licensing chip manufacturing technology to them.

In a separate agreement, the US government will take a 4 percent stake in GlobalFoundries, bringing its total ownership of the chipmaker to about 7 percent, GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters. Breen said GlobalFoundries would manage customer relationships, and initial customers for the New York factories include Japan’s Renesas Electronics and iPhone maker Apple.

“We definitely would like to give priority to US and Japanese customers,” he said. “Ultimately, I expect other companies that aren’t US and Japanese will also be part of the demand, but we’ll obviously go through a process after announcement to finalize the exact who gets what over what timeframe.” Japan has so far announced two batches of projects worth over USD100 billion combined under the investment scheme.

Under the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flows from investments will be split evenly between the two countries until a specific allocation is reached, after which 90 percent will go to the US.

GlobalFoundries’ Breen said that at least some of the capital investment by Japan will flow back to chip-manufacturing toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron and other Japanese firms that along with US rivals dominate the supply chain. “Obviously, we have a strong interest in the Japanese equipment suppliers to be part of it,” Breen said. “We will be very open-minded, but we’ll definitely engage very much with the Japanese ecosystem because they have great technologies.”

news.title: ‘No Kings’ movement seeks to boost early voting
news.text:
WASHINGTON: As Americans begin casting their ballots in the midterm elections, the prominent “No Kings” anti-Trump movement is organizing thousands of rallies Saturday to get voters fired up.

“No Kings” has more than 3,000 events planned across the United States for its fourth iteration since US President Donald Trump returned to office, this time with a special twist for the November 3 vote.

Dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early,” the events on Saturday aim to get out the vote rather than protest the actions of Trump and his Republican administration.

“It’s a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard,” organizers said in a statement.

Saturday’s itinerary varies widely depending on the location, from a music festival in Los Angeles and a march to the Supreme Court in Washington, to family-friendly workshops in Chicago and election observer training in Atlanta.

“No Kings: Early Vote will be thousands of joyful celebrations of our right to vote across the country,” said Deirdre Schifeling, the chief political and advocacy officer of the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the partner organizations behind Saturday’s events.

Although Tuesday, November 3 is election day, most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

Alma Couverthie, who oversees grassroots organizing efforts for democracy watchdog organization Common Cause, said the point of the upcoming “No Kings” rallies is “reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service, and an act of joy.”

“This Saturday, October 17, will be a celebration of our collective power. Walk together to the polls. Organize rides. Bring your neighbors, friends, and family,” she urged participants.

Trump has openly criticized the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results — especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is quite likely.

By advocating for voting early, the “No Kings” organizers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance once election day rolls around.

“The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question,” Couverthie said.
