news.title: Canada races to seal India trade pact by year-end, deepen EU ties
news.text:
NEW DELHI: Canada is racing to seal a trade pact with India and deepen ties with the European Union as it seeks to reduce reliance on the US amid President Donald Trump’s protectionist trade policy, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said on Wednesday.

The push is central to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify trade and strengthen ties with the EU, China and other countries even as Ottawa seeks to maintain cooperation with Washington on trade, defence and security.

“The Comprehensive Economic Partnership agreement with India is part of our trade diversification strategy, and yes, we aim to conclude it by the end of the year,” Anand told Reuters in an interview at the Canadian High Commission in New Delhi.

“Canada has a goal of doubling non-US trade over the next 10 years,” Anand said. Canada and the EU are expected to discuss cooperation on critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence at a summit later this month, building on trade ties under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), Anand said.

Canada is also broadening its trade partnerships, having signed a free trade agreement with Indonesia last year and is looking to sign a pact with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2026. Ottawa has concluded 15 trade agreements covering 51 countries and 1.5 billion consumers, she said.

“It is really about our national resilience and our sovereignty,” Anand said. “We need to ensure that we are not reliant on any one country for the economic resilience that our country has been able to exhibit.”

INDIA TRADE PACT

Negotiations on the India agreement were progressing well, Anand said, adding that Indian trade negotiators had visited Canada last week and Canadian Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu was in India with a business delegation. Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had discussed the agreement, she said. Modi is expected to visit Canada in December.

Canada says a deal could more than double bilateral goods and services trade to USD70 billion annually by 2030 from the USD30.4 billion recorded in 2025. Goods trade with India reached USD10.9 billion in 2025, with Canadian exports falling 26.5 percent from 2024, while imports from India rose by 18.9 percent.

A CUSD2.6 billion (USD1.8 billion) uranium supply agreement between Canadian company Cameco and India, signed earlier this year, was one tangible outcome of closer cooperation, she said.

In one example of deepening economic ties, Canada’s Fairfax Financial Holdings has agreed to buy a majority stake in India’s IDBI Bank in a deal valued at 528.78 billion rupees (USD5.56 billion), in what will be India’s biggest cross-border bank deal.

The two countries are seeking to rebuild ties following a diplomatic dispute over the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada.

Anand said restoring relations was a gradual process, with national security and the rule of law central to the effort. “We are speaking about our sovereignty and our resilience, and we need to continue to focus on that,” she said.
news.summary:
NEW DELHI: Canada is racing to seal a trade pact with India and deepen ties with the European Union as it seeks to reduce reliance on the US amid President Donald Trump’s protectionist trade policy, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said on Wednesday.


The push is central to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify trade and strengthen ties with the EU, China and other countries even as Ottawa seeks to maintain cooperation with Washington on trade, defence and security.


“The Comprehensive Economic Partnership agreement with India is part of our trade diversification strategy, and yes, we aim to conclude it by the end of the year,” Anand told Reuters in an interview at the Canadian High Commission in New Delhi.


“Canada has a goal of doubling non-US trade over the next 10 years,” Anand said. Canada and the EU are expected to discuss cooperation on critical minerals, energy and artificial intelligence at a summit later this month, building on trade ties under the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Joe Manchin Warns Democrats Trump Investigations Could Cost Them in 2028
news.text: Former Senator Joe Manchin has warned Democrats that launching investigations into President Donald Trump if they win control of Congress could backfire politically and pave the way for a Republican takeover in 2028. “If they start with investigations, Michael, it’s over,” Manchin told CNN host Michael Smerconish on Saturday’s edition of Smerconish. “They’re going to tee up everything in 2028 for a Republican takeover completely.” The former West Virginia senator urged Democrats to focus instead on lowering Americans’ cost of living if they make gains in November’s midterm elections, arguing that they should send Trump legislation aimed at helping voters and force the president to decide whether to veto it. Manchin’s warning comes as Democrats debate how they would use congressional power if they retake the House, including whether to launch investigations of Trump and his administration that could ultimately lead to a third impeachment of the president. Some Democrats have already called for Trump to be impeached, while others have warned that another impeachment fight could distract from the party’s message on affordability and hand Republicans a political weapon. Joe Manchin Warns Democrats Against Trump Investigations Speaking to Smerconish, Manchin said Democrats would be better served by concentrating on legislation designed to ease the financial pressures facing American families. “The problem now is, is that if they go in, Democrats go in strictly talking about all I’m concerned about right now is reducing the cost for you to be able to live a life that you can take care of yourself and your family,” he said. Manchin argued that Democrats should advance policies even if Trump opposes them, putting the onus on the president to reject measures the party can present to voters as beneficial. “If they can do that, they’re fine,” he said. “If they can’t, and they’re just consumed with retaliation and retribution, which is what we’ve been seeing for the last two years, that’s not what the American people want or need right now.” The warning pushes the debate beyond November’s midterm elections. Manchin argued that how Democrats govern after a potential midterm victory could have consequences in 2028, when Trump will be unable to seek another term. It also puts Manchin alongside Democrats who have cautioned against allowing impeachment or investigations to overshadow economic issues, although his warning goes further by predicting a “Republican takeover” if Democrats make that mistake. Democrats Weigh Trump Investigations if They Win House Democrats are increasingly grappling with what a new House majority should do about Trump. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has declined to rule out impeachment, telling PBS last month: “We certainly haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out.” Jeffries said Democrats would investigate potential wrongdoing, “follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution” and “let the chips fall where they may.” Jeffries, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar drew that line in September after Democratic Representative Al Green of Texas brought another impeachment resolution against Trump. “Impeachment is a sacred constitutional vehicle designed to hold a corrupt executive accountable for abuse of power, breaking the law and violating the public trust,” the three leaders said in a joint statement. But, they added, such an effort “traditionally requires a comprehensive investigative process,” which they said had not occurred. Less than two weeks later, Democratic Representative Steve Cohen of Tennessee introduced another effort, consisting of 26 articles of impeachment alleging misconduct by Trump across issues including immigration, the Iran war, tariffs, federal spending, presidential pardons and alleged personal financial benefit from the presidency. Cohen has acknowledged that his effort is unlikely to advance under the current Republican-controlled Congress. “I know they won't go anywhere, but I'm not going to stop standing up for my constituents and for democracy,” he told Nexstar. Democrats Clash Over Trump Impeachment Before Midterms Manchin is not alone in warning his former party about the political risks of another impeachment battle. Former Obama White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel answered “Short answer: No” when asked on NBC News’ Meet the Press on October 4 whether Democrats should impeach Trump if they regain the House. “It’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight,” Emanuel said. He has instead advocated investigating alleged corruption before pursuing a broader ethics package. Former Democratic Representative Joe Cunningham of South Carolina previously told Newsweek that congressional Democrats risk allowing impeachment to overwhelm the rest of their agenda. “If Democrats initiate an impeachment process, it will consume the oxygen in Washington and overshadow virtually everything else they are trying to accomplish for Americans,” Cunningham said. “The Democratic Party needs to be known for what it is fighting for, not simply what it is fighting against.” That argument closely parallels Manchin’s emphasis on affordability, although Manchin’s remarks Saturday were directed more broadly at investigations rather than impeachment alone. Trump Impeachment Divides Democrats in Key 2026 Races The disagreement has also surfaced in competitive Senate races ahead of the midterms. Former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown has said he would not support Trump’s impeachment, while New Hampshire Representative Chris Pappas said impeachment “should not come at the expense of the need to focus on the cost-of-living crisis and addressing the healthcare challenges that New Hampshire is facing.” Josh Turek, the Democratic candidate challenging Republican Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa’s Senate race, has said he has “no interest” in pursuing impeachment. “I think that we need to look forward and not back,” Turek said. In Kansas, Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has similarly said he is “not going to Washington to hold trials.” “I’m going to Washington to fight for the people of Kansas and make life better for them,” he said. But other Democrats have taken a different position. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has said he sees multiple potential impeachable offenses by Trump, while arguing that enforcement of the law rather than political retribution should drive any action. Minnesota Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan has been more direct, saying impeachment “is absolutely on the table and I will absolutely be on board for that.” Could Donald Trump Be Impeached Again? A Democratic takeover of the House would fundamentally change the impeachment arithmetic, but not necessarily make Trump’s removal likely. The House can impeach a president by a simple majority. Conviction and removal from office, however, require a two-thirds vote among senators present, meaning Republican support would almost certainly be required regardless of the midterm results. Trump himself has recently raised the prospect of another impeachment if Democrats take control of Congress. Asked outside the White House on October 2 what a third impeachment would mean for him, he replied: “Well, I don’t know, but I’m getting good at it.” He went on to dismiss his previous impeachments as “fake,” saying: “But with me, they like to do it.” Trump was impeached twice during his first term. The House impeached him in December 2019 on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress following an investigation into his dealings with Ukraine. The Senate acquitted him in February 2020. He was impeached again in January 2021 on a charge of incitement of insurrection following the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol and was again acquitted by the Senate. Public opinion does not make the question straightforward for Democrats. A Strength in Numbers/Verasight poll conducted April 10-14 found that 55 percent of Americans supported the House impeaching Trump, while 37 percent opposed it and 8 percent said they did not know. The poll underscores the competing pressures Democrats could face if they win the House: public support for impeachment alongside concerns that investigations could overshadow their governing agenda. Trump and Republicans have already sought to make that prospect part of their midterm argument. House Speaker Mike Johnson has warned that Democrats would impeach Trump if Republicans lose their majority. For Manchin, however, the larger danger for Democrats comes after the midterms. A Democratic victory would give the party an opportunity to demonstrate that it can govern, he argued, while becoming “consumed with retaliation and retribution” could instead help Republicans return to power in 2028.
news.summary: Joe Manchin says Democrats risk a Republican takeover in 2028 if they prioritize Trump investigations.
news.author: Steve Mollman

news.title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Hormuz within a week
news.text:
Iran could restore normal shipping through the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington accepts a peace plan proposed by Tehran last month, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said. The terms were previously rejected by US President Donald Trump.

The Islamic Republic remains “committed to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi told a ministerial meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation on Saturday, blaming disruptions to shipping through the key waterway on the “aggressive actions” of the US and Israel.

”Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” the minister said. “The choice now rests with the United States.”

“This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation,” Araghchi added.

Tehran has offered to restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its naval blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also demanding an end to hostilities “on all fronts,” including Israel’s military operations in Gaza and Lebanon.

Last month, Trump rejected Iran’s terms as “unacceptable.” He argued that the US retained full control over the strait and held a stronger negotiating position, while Iran was desperate to reach an agreement because it was “losing so badly.”

The US president has hinted that he could resume strikes, while American media outlets have reported that Pentagon officials and national security advisers briefed him on options involving the use of a massive conventional bomb nicknamed the “Mother of All Bombs.” However, Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have ruled out attacks on Iran before the US midterms on November 3 and Israel’s parliamentary elections on October 27, respectively.

Iran closed the waterway, which handles around a quarter of global seaborne oil and LNG trade, shortly after the US and Israel launched their bombing campaign on February 28. Iranian forces have since fired on vessels traveling along routes designated by the US Navy, which Tehran considers illegal.

Two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said. The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride also sank after striking a mine earlier this week, while another cargo vessel hit a mine but managed to reach port safely.

The prolonged disruption of shipping through Hormuz has driven up global energy prices and fueled inflation concerns. Brent crude surged to a five-month high on Friday, settling at $109.86 per barrel, up 3.7%, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate climbed above $100. Analysts have warned that uncertainty over Middle Eastern supplies is keeping a significant risk premium in oil prices, which could ease if Washington and Tehran reach an agreement restoring normal shipping.
news.summary:
Tehran says it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington accepts its peace plan, which Trump previously rejected

news.title: Schoolchildren 'brainwashed by left-wing BBC': Demand for inquiry as education website used by millions encourages pupils to back contentious open borders and Net Zero policies
news.text:
Schoolchildren 'brainwashed by left-wing BBC': Demand for inquiry as education website used by millions encourages pupils to back contentious open borders and Net Zero policies

By MARK HOOKHAM, ASSISTANT EDITOR (INVESTIGATIONS)

Published: 23:29 BST, 17 October 2026 | Updated: 00:00 BST, 18 October 2026

The BBC was accused of 'brainwashing' children after a Mail on Sunday investigation revealed its education website is pushing 'extreme' Left-wing views on migration, Net Zero and inequality to millions of pupils.

BBC Bitesize – which is promoted by almost every UK state school – encourages children to play an online game called Increasing Immigration, in which they are rewarded for choosing 'open borders' and granting an amnesty to illegal migrants.

The website also suggests that those who voice concerns that migrants will take jobs from local people are 'prejudiced' and makes a string of claims about the economic benefits of migration. 

Pupils are encouraged to campaign for controversial Net Zero policies and join human rights groups such as Amnesty International – while the website praises the divisive Black Lives Matter movement and Left-wing activists such as Greta Thunberg.

Our revelations will fuel allegations of political bias at the broadcaster and follows a series of scandals that have damaged the BBC's reputation, including its doctoring of a Donald Trump speech.

It comes as the Corporation faces a pivotal moment in its history, with Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy expected to publish a White Paper on its charter renewal before Christmas. 

BBC director general Matt Brittin has pledged to tackle bias by rolling out technology that monitors how often certain words or phrases are used.

Danny Cohen, a former controller of BBC television, last night called for an urgent investigation into our findings. 

The BBC was accused of 'brainwashing' children after a Mail on Sunday investigation revealed its education website is pushing 'extreme' Left-wing views on migration, Net Zero and inequality to millions of pupils

BBC Bitesize – which is promoted by almost every UK state school – encourages children to play an online game called Increasing Immigration, in which they are rewarded for choosing 'open borders' and granting an amnesty to illegal migrants

'The BBC needs to explain why its educational website is pushing extreme Left-wing ideologies to schoolchildren,' he said. 'There is such a lack of balance in so many areas of the BBC's output that it cannot be seriously defended as coincidental.'

Launched in 1998, BBC Bitesize is one of the biggest education websites in Britain, with half of all children aged between four and 16 saying they use it. Almost 1.7 million pupils access it every week.

BBC bosses have hailed the service as a key part of the broadcaster's founding 'Reithian' values to 'inform, educate and entertain'.

The MoS investigation reviewed material on BBC Bitesize for pre-GCSE secondary school pupils aged 11 to 14.

In one extraordinary example, pupils are encouraged to play a game called Increasing Immigration, making decisions aimed at boosting the number of incomers.

Each option comes with a budget 'cost' and once they've chosen, they find out the effects on the economy, public health and the environment.

Instructions for the game, hosted on the Roblox platform, state: 'We don't have enough people of working age to keep our society running smoothly. We should try to attract migrant workers and incorporate them into our economy.'

In one scenario, pupils are told that 'a few' immigrants are living here without proper visas or permission and can either deport them or grant them an amnesty. If they choose deportation they will lose one point on the economy and one on public health – and are warned: 'This can be potentially dangerous for them [the immigrants]. Don't expect this to be unchallenged!'

But those who opt to grant an amnesty are told 'this will make them very happy' and win two points in the same categories.

In a second scenario, geography pupils are told that allowing people to pass through the border easily 'could really help grow our economy'. They are offered the option of 'open borders' – which results in their economy score rising by three points and public health by two points – or to vote that such a policy would be 'too radical', winning them no points.

Those who opt for open borders receive the optimistic message: 'I'm excited to see where this goes!' In contrast, pupils who select 'too radical' are told: 'Perhaps you're right to be cautious.'

BBC director general Matt Brittin has pledged to tackle bias by rolling out technology that monitors how often certain words or phrases are used

A third example involves 'poorly-paid, demanding' jobs available in food processing. Pupils are told hiring locals costs the fictional budget two points, but employing migrants costs one. In this scenario, each option boosts the economy by the same amount, but hiring migrants costs players less.

The BBC this weekend said players are not rewarded for choosing political positions and that points are also awarded for training local people and for closing borders.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott last night demanded the BBC remove the game from its website. 'The BBC has crossed a line,' she said. 'They have a duty to remain impartial, and yet they are using learning tools as a vehicle to push a Left-wing political agenda onto young children.

'Advocating open borders encourages illegal small boat crossings. These are the type of toxic resources dressed up as education which should be nowhere near the classroom.'

Accompanying material for teachers explains the game is set in 'Southern Europe', although this is unclear when playing.

Elsewhere on the Bitesize website, learning material is littered with contested claims about the economic benefits of migration.

Citizenship pupils in Northern Ireland are told that while immigrants can put pressure on housing and hospital waiting lists, they also 'contribute more in tax income that they use in services' and 'make a significant contribution to the economy: they fill skills gaps, pay taxes, and spend money'.

Geography pupils in Wales, meanwhile, are told that migrants pump a 'staggering amount of money' into the economy.

The website does not, however, make clear that the economic impact of migrants varies greatly depending on their skills and the type of visa they have been issued.

Those on skilled worker visas do contribute more in tax than they use in services but care workers and the immigrant relatives of British citizens have a negative fiscal impact, Oxford University's respected Migration Observatory has found.

The Northern Ireland study material also states: 'Some people may think that migrants take jobs from local people. This view likely arises from prejudice.'

Another part of the website lists twice as many benefits for migration compared to disadvantages.

BBC Bitesize also appears to be advocating a world without borders. A video for Welsh geography students states: 'As technology evolves... the question remains: can we learn to live with globalisation? And with it, fulfil the promise of a truly borderless world.'

Former BBC boss Mr Cohen added: 'Parents ought to be deeply concerned that the BBC is encouraging children to conform to extreme ideas such as open borders. It is yet another unacceptable failure of the BBC's requirement to ensure impartiality.'

A video on the website also describes the contentious Net Zero policy as an 'important goal' and suggests that pupils could 'petition your local government to act'. Another video, for students in Wales, states: 'For us to reach Net Zero in Wales, we'll have to do things differently. We may need to fly less, eat less meat or stick to sustainably farmed meat.'

But mainstream politicians have rejected that idea. Sir Keir Starmer last year said tackling climate change 'does not mean telling people how to run their lives'.

BBC Bitesize material also hails a string of Left-wing and progressive 'political' icons, including climate activist Greta Thunberg and 1980s campaign group Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners.

BBC Bitesize material also hails a string of Left-wing and progressive 'political' icons, including climate activist Greta Thunberg (pictured) and 1980s campaign group Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners

A video asks if pupils joined Ms Thunberg's school protests, when pupils skipped Friday classes to campaign against climate change.

Elsewhere it says that a statue to US anti-slavery campaigner Frederick Douglass in Belfast is a 'reminder that anti-racism movements such as Black Lives Matter in Belfast and across Ireland are one with the movements of the rest of the world'.'

The website also says Black Lives Matter 'campaigns for freedom, justice and equality'. It does not, however, acknowledge how the movement in the UK became highly contentious after it was hijacked by far-Left activists who want to tear down capitalism and abolish the police.

In another video about reducing inequality, the presenter states that 'the world becomes a fairer place when we take every cause as our own' and, over footage of a Pride flag, says 'I will always be an ally to those shouting for equality'.

It also shows demonstrations featuring placards emblazoned with 'Black Muslim Lives Matter' and 'Refugees Welcome'.

In a different section about slavery, Bitesize tells pupils to 'join and campaign' with groups such as Amnesty International.

The UK arm of the charity was widely criticised earlier this year after describing gender-critical organisations and a woman's refuge backed by J. K. Rowling as 'anti-rights' groups. It later withdrew the report and referred itself to the Charity Commission.

Alex Burghart, Shadow Cabinet Office Secretary, said: 'The BBC was set up to inform, educate and entertain –- not misinform, re-educate and brainwash.' And former Tory Education Secretary Gavin Williamson MP said: 'The mask has slipped and the BBC has yet again betrayed its rampant Left-wing political agenda. The state broadcaster brainwashing children using a homework game is like something from a North Korean re-education camp.'

A BBC spokesman said: 'BBC Bitesize works with educational consultants to develop resources that help young people explore and understand a wide range of topics, aligned to the respective curriculums across the UK.

'While we don't accept the characterisation of Bitesize in this story, we regularly review content to ensure it remains relevant and to ensure it meets the BBC's editorial standards and will review these examples in that context.'

Director-general Matt Brittin warned in July that the BBC faced a 'moment of real jeopardy' after the number of households paying the licence fee fell by more than 500,000 in the past year.

Additional reporting: Gabriel Millard-Clothier

news.summary: BBC Bitesize encourages children to play an online game called Increasing Immigration, in which they are rewarded for choosing 'open borders' and granting an amnesty to illegal migrants.

news.title: 'No Kings' Rallies Return, Send Trump a Midterm Warning: 'Democracy Under Attack'
news.text: Thousands of people took part in a fresh round of "No Kings" events across the United States on Saturday, with organisers urging voters to cast their ballots early ahead of November's midterm elections. The gatherings were billed as non-partisan events focused on voter participation, marking a shift from earlier demonstrations that had targeted a range of policies under President Donald Trump, including immigration raids, budget cuts and government job cuts. However, many participants also voiced opposition to the Trump administration's agenda, echoing the criticism heard at previous "No Kings" rallies. Organisers encouraged smaller, locally focused gatherings rather than large-scale demonstrations. More than 2,500 events were planned across the country, including a virtual option. "Voting early is how we use our power," the national "No Kings" coalition said on its website. The coalition includes about 200 organisations, among them the American Civil Liberties Union and the League of Women Voters. With the midterm elections approaching, organisers urged people to visit early voting sites or submit absentee ballots. Here is how the events unfolded in three US cities. Atlanta At Piedmont Park, speakers urged people to vote early and encourage others to do the same. Gerald Griggs, a civil rights lawyer, invoked figures including Martin Luther King Jr and John Lewis as he called on the crowd to mobilise voters. "In the spirit of these civil rights icons and the nameless foot soldiers, it's our time," he said. "So go vote early, contact five of your friends, and tell them go vote early." Some participants expressed concern over Trump's efforts to overturn his 2020 election defeat in Georgia. Felicia Murray Jackson, who led a march from the park to a church, spoke about the death of her older sister, who was killed in February when a man fleeing immigration agents crashed into her car. "I don't want to hear you tell me how sorry you are for my loss — I want to hear you say, I took your loss straight to the ballot box," she told the crowd. "We're going to take human trafficking, child rape and the Epstein files straight to the ballot box," she added. Oklahoma City Dozens of people gathered outside Mayflower Congregational Church in Oklahoma City, where voter registration had closed on 9 October. Participants held signs along Portland Avenue and filled out postcards reminding voters about the midterm elections. Nina Lawrence, an organiser, said the initiative aimed to address Oklahoma's low voter turnout. "We can send them to voters who need an extra nudge, and a reminder that voting in the midterms is just as important as voting in the presidential election," she said. Lu Eyerman, a spokeswoman for the grassroots voter movement Indivisible, said the campaign was also intended to prepare people for developments in the run-up to the November election. "We want to be prepared to help in whatever way we can," she said. Dallas Near Pacific Plaza in downtown Dallas, Stephanie Williams of the Black Voters Matter Fund led chants opposing the administration. "Our democracy is under attack!" she shouted, prompting the crowd to respond: "We fight back!" Williams highlighted the impact of government policies on everyday expenses, including healthcare, food assistance through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and electricity bills. "We have marched. We have rallied. We said, ‘No Kings.' Today, we're going to move from protest to power," she said. People across the lawn held signs bearing messages such as "Save democracy" and "Be a hero, vote!" Among those attending were Pam and Royce Mitchell, both 73, who have been married for 51 years and were attending their first "No Kings" rally. Pam Mitchell, a retired kindergarten teacher, said the couple had previously supported former Republican President George W Bush but were now Democrats. She said the current political climate was no longer simply a matter of Democrats versus Republicans.
news.summary: Over 2,500 events were organized, including smaller local gatherings. Notable speakers emphasized the importance of mobilizing voters, referencing civil rights icons
news.author: Rounak Bagchi

news.title: Under fire, Rep. Ilhan Omar demands return of seized items, including sister’s phone
news.text:
Family text messages are among the information that federal officials are reviewing as they continue their investigation into U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, which came into public view this week with the federal raid of her Washington, D.C., home, according to anonymous sources who spoke to the New York Times. 

The messages came from a phone that belonged to one of Omar’s sisters and was previously seized by officials, the report said. The texts were among the information used to convince a federal judge to carry out the raid on Omar’s residence on Monday.

The Justice Department did not respond to requests by the Minnesota Star Tribune to confirm the seizure of the sister’s phone. Omar’s office also did not comment on the phone seizure.

The full scope of the investigation into Omar and other details remain unclear. A source familiar with the probe has said that officials have so far confiscated Omar’s phone, laptop, notebooks and passport and that some of her family members, including her sister, have been subpoenaed. The source said authorities have not subpoenaed her children or her husband, Tim Mynett.

Advertisement

Lawyers for Omar raised concerns over the raid of her residence and demanded the return of seized items in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by the Star Tribune. They described the search as “neither justified nor lawful.”

The investigation into the immigration status of Omar, a longtime critic of President Donald Trump, prompted cheers from the right but concern from the left and independent observers.

Omar has said that she naturalized as a U.S. citizen before turning 18. Her family fled the civil war in Somalia before arriving in Minnesota in 1997 when she was 14 years old.

Documents released in 2019 showed discrepancies in her marriage history, long the basis for Republican accusations that she had illegally immigrated. But the Minnesota Star Tribune did not find conclusive evidence of wrongdoing. The Washington Post reported that federal officials scrutinized Omar during Trump’s first term, but ultimately declined to pursue a full investigation because of insufficient evidence.
news.summary: The federal probe into Omar’s immigration status involves family text messages and seized personal items.
news.author: Cole Reynolds,Sarah Nelson,Sydney Kashiwagi

news.title: I Know Who Will Go Next in Trump’s Reign of Chaos: Author
news.text:
The shocking shakeup at the highest levels of the Trump administration this week may not be over yet, the president’s longtime biographer predicts.

After Katie Zacharia was fired as press secretary and Kimberly Guilfoyle was axed as the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, author Michael Wolff says he believes White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles could be next—despite Trump’s repeated assurances his loyal enforcer is here to stay.

“I think it’s very possible,” Wolff said of a Wiles departure or firing. “I mean, I think it’s also possible that she’s telling Donald Trump that she’s making noises that she’s gonna go. If I were the chief of staff and had the last two years of an administration, and then losing the midterms, it’s a very good time to go.”

He continued, “As all people in the White House are always doing, she’s thinking about, ‘What next? What do I get out of this? Do I write a book? How do I make money? What’s the best place for me to be,’ and not what is necessarily best for the White House.” 

Trump, 80, insisted on Friday there is “zero chance” he is considering booting Wiles, 69, after she made headlines for a reported rift with the president over selecting Zacharia as press secretary. 

The Daily Mail previously reported that Wiles wanted CNN’s conservative commentator Scott Jennings for the role, but Trump ultimately chose Zacharia. Politico later revealed Trump is phoning his allies to solicit their opinions on Wiles, fueling speculation he could oust his top MAGA 2.0 adviser.

“The Susie Wiles story was a fake story,” Trump told reporters of the Politico report. “It’s been incredible. We’ve had maybe the most successful first two years, and if not, even two years, in the history of the presidency. She’s been my chief of staff. She’s smart. She’s tough. She just went through a lot with the cancer surgery and the whole thing, and she recovered, fully recovered.”

“She’s phenomenal,” he added. “Susie is here, and she’s gonna be here for a long time.”

But Wolff told his Inside Trump’s Head co-host Joanna Coles that Trump’s statement is a flashing red light.

“I mean, that’s a danger sign,” he said. “So if he is saying that, if he feels the need to say that, it’s because she’s on shaky ground.”

Wolff speculated that Wiles could become the administration’s scapegoat if Republicans lose the crucial November midterm elections.

“Poor Katie Zacharia, it’s not really her fault. It’s Donald Trump’s fault. He picked her out of nowhere without preparation,” Wolff said. “Trump said, ‘Oh, yeah, I like the way she looks, I like that look. Let’s get her,’ bypassing Susie Wiles, an indication that—I mean, Trump is in charge, wants to be in charge, resents the suggestion that anyone else actually might be in charge. I would say it’s a pretty good chance, maybe a fair chance, maybe inevitable that Susie Wiles goes.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.

Zacharia was fired after just five days, setting an embarrassing new record for the shortest tenure of a press secretary. The 41-year-old conservative commentator suffered a brutal week marked by a car-crash press briefing and questions over legal pedigree, punctuated by her struggling to answer tough questions in appearances on Fox News.

On Thursday, Zacharia sought to save face on an interview with Sean Hannity. But the Fox News star went hard on her—and even Trump admitted, “Sean was a little bit tough.”

Insiders later told Politico that the disastrous interview was a “sanctioned hit” that Wiles helped organize.

“[White House spokesperson] Danielle [Alvarez] and Susie fed her to Hannity,” one source familiar with the matter told the outlet, adding that Wiles and Hannity are friendly.

A senior White House official countered, “Susie and Sean do talk, but Susie did not need to feed her to Sean or anybody else. It’s not her style.”

New episodes of incomparable insight into the psyche of the world’s most talked-about man drop every Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday evening on YouTube and Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday mornings on other podcast platforms.

news.title: Trump’s decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen
news.text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.

Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia’s Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the US that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

“I think it’s clear Russia is the aggressor, and we’ve got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia,” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said in an interview with The Associated Press. “So it’s not the first thing I would be doing.”

“Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russia’s economy could be revived.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”

Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.

Trump’s actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia’s ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelensky, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the US lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions.

The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington.

Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law

It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as a way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin’s four-year war against Ukraine.

But even as Zelensky had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham’s death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago.

Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law’s provisions were to be effective Sunday.

Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the US, where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters are saying affordability issues are a top concern.

Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal.

New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump’s diesel deal with Putin. “At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine,” Meeks said in a statement.

He called the deal “corrupt” and said it “goes against everything the United States stands for.”

On Saturday, he said that “Congress is not helpless” and must act.

Graham’s legacy on the line

Graham’s sister, Darline Graham of South Carolina, helped ensure Senate passage of the bill, once she was appointed by the state’s governor to fill her brother’s seat.

She is now running against Democrat Annie Andrews in a tight race. Trump is expected in the state next week to rally voters.

“Look, the president and I share the same goal, which is to end the war, to get gas and diesel prices down, and the sanctions bill is one of the tools he can use to do that,” Darline Graham said at a campaign stop Saturday.

“It’s up to him whether or not he chooses to use it. Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she said, “because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”

Like her brother, who often publicly parted ways with the president, Darline Graham said she and Trump can have their differences.

“I am proud of it to help get across the finish line. It meant a lot to Lindsey,” she said. “But you know, like Lindsey, he disagreed with the president sometimes they had that relationship where they could agree to disagree sometimes. And I think that just happens.”

news.title: Trump approves emergency declaration for CNMI
news.text:
PRESIDENT Donald J. Trump has approved a federal emergency declaration for the CNMI for Typhoon Champi, making federal help available for Saipan, Tinian and Rota.

The declaration, FEMA-3658-EM, was approved on Oct. 17. That was one day after Gov. David M. Apatang submitted the request on Oct. 16, according to the CNMI Joint Information Center.

“We are grateful to President Donald J. Trump, the White House, FEMA, and our federal partners for acting quickly on our request,” Apatang said. He said the declaration gives the CNMI the federal support it needs for residents of the three islands during the response to Champi.

The governor also pointed to the hardships the islands have faced in recent months.

“This has been an incredibly difficult year for our islands. Our people have endured storm after storm, and each time they have shown remarkable strength and resilience. This federal assistance comes at a critical time,” he said.

The declaration authorizes the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide help with emergency measures under Title V of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. That help is meant to save lives, protect property, public health and safety, and lessen or avert the threat of a catastrophe in the designated areas.

Andrew F. Grant of FEMA’s National Federal Coordinating Officer Program has been named federal coordinating officer for response operations in the affected areas.

Officials said more designations may be made later if the Commonwealth requests them and further evaluation shows they are needed.

Champi was upgraded to a super typhoon early Sunday. At 7 a.m., it was about 90 miles southwest of Rota and 165 miles southwest of Saipan, with maximum sustained winds of 150 mph. Rota remains under Typhoon Condition I, and Saipan and Tinian are under Typhoon Condition III.

news.title: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a US mass shooting
news.text:
Few mass shootings in the U.S. end like the deadly attack on an Oregon elementary school: with an armed civilian opening fire on the gunman.

President Donald Trump joined others Friday in praising a father of two girls who confronted a teenage gunman during the attack at Silver Rail Elementary School, which killed three students and a teacher. Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened by firing his own weapon after the shooting began at his daughters’ school in the town of Bend.

“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter who had a .40-caliber pistol legally stored in his vehicle, entered the school, heard shots and fired his gun after seeing a teacher fighting with the shooter, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

Cases like the Oregon intervention remain rare, according to the Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training Center at Texas State University.

The ALERRT center tracked what it calls “active attack” incidents where the perpetrator used firearms, blades or vehicles from 2000 to 2025.

Out of 634 cases studied, 374 ended before police arrived. Among those, 29 ended when armed civilians shot the attacker. In another 31 incidents, civilians subdued the attacker by some other method, such as wrestling them to the ground or removing the weapon.

“They recognize they may be the only way to stop it before law enforcement arrives,” said James Keith, a spokesperson for the center.

The heroic “good guy with a gun” who can stop an attack even before law enforcement can arrive has long been a rallying cry by gun rights advocates, arguing that armed citizens can act as a first line of self-defense and public protection. In some cases, the person who intervenes has had law enforcement or military training. Other times they are just people who reacted in a moment of chaos.

In some states, lawmakers have sought to put armed citizens in position to head off an attack as soon as possible in some public spaces.

Texas created a school marshal program in 2013 to allow trained teachers and staff to carry concealed firearms on campus. It expanded safety programs and requirements for armed security and personnel at schools after mass shootings at a high school near Houston in 2018, and at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022.

Texas has some of the least restrictive gun control laws in the country, according to the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. The group rates Oregon among the strongest.

Some prominent examples of armed citizens who confronted gunmen to help stop mass shootings:

Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out

A gunman killed three people and wounded seven more at an In-N-Out Burger on Aug. 3. Law enforcement authorities said the gunman may have killed more if not for an off-duty officer who was a customer at the restaurant, and an armed civilian who exchanged fire with the gunman.

Jordan Salinas said he didn’t hesitate to grab his gun and confront the gunman when he saw people fleeing the restaurant and heard gunfire. Under return fire, the gunman retreated and ultimately killed himself.

“He did not like it when bullets started flying both ways,” Salinas told the Idaho Statesman. “There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it.”

White Settlement, Texas, church shooting

In December 2019, a man wearing a disguise and a trench coat pulled out a shotgun and killed two people during a Sunday service at West Freeway Church of Christ before he was killed by Jack Wilson, a 71-year-old firearms instructor who had also been a reserve sheriff’s deputy.

Wilson stayed calm as worshippers scrambled for cover.

“The only clear shot I had was his head because I still had people in the pews that were not all the way down as low as they could. That was my one shot,” Wilson said in 2019.

Sutherland Springs, Texas, church shooting

A gunman killed 26 people at a small-town church in 2017. Stephen Willeford, a former National Rifle Association instructor who lived across the street, grabbed his rifle and ran in his bare feet to open fire at the attacker, wounding him.

The gunman fled and Willeford flagged down a passing driver. The two men chased after the gunman, who eventually killed himself.

“I kept hearing the shots: pop, pop, pop” when the gunfire started at the church, Willeford said in 2017. “And I knew every one of those shots represented someone, that it was aimed at someone.”
news.summary: Few mass shootings in the U.S. end like the deadly attack on an Oregon elementary school: with an armed civilian opening fire on the gunman....

news.title: New Kristi Noem Hunting Photo With Gun, Dog Sparks Concerned Comments
news.text: Former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem bid South Dakota a happy pheasant hunting season on Saturday with a post on X that included a photo of her in hunting gear holding a gun while next to a dog, prompting a slew of concerned comments on the internet. The post comes a day after a State Department official said that Noem was no longer special envoy to the Shield of the Americas coalition, which is a role she filled after being fired as DHS secretary in March. According to a document shared by Noem on X on Friday, the position was "always a six-month appointment," and Noem remains a senior adviser within the State Department. Newsweek reached out to representatives for Noem by email and to the U.S. Department of State by online contact form for comment on Saturday afternoon. Who Is Kristi Noem? Noem served as governor of South Dakota from 2019 to 2025 before leaving the role to become President Donald Trump's DHS secretary. A prominent Trump ally and avid hunter, she was once considered a leading contender to be his running mate in 2024. However, that speculation faded after the publication of excerpts from her memoir No Going Back, in which she recounted shooting her 14-month-old dog, Cricket, after deeming it "untrainable," sparking widespread backlash. She returned to the headlines earlier this year when The Daily Mail reported that her husband, Bryon Noem, had allegedly led a double life that included wearing fake breasts and communicating with fetish models online. Noem filed for divorce from her husband in September. Kristi Noem Special Envoy Role Ends On Friday, news broke that Noem's role as special envoy to the Shield of the Americas had ended. "Shield of the Americas" was a Trump administration security initiative focused on the Western Hemisphere, aimed at countering drug trafficking, transnational criminal networks and illegal migration. As special envoy, Noem represented the administration as it coordinated with regional leaders on security and enforcement efforts. In that role, she reported to Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. She is now senior adviser to Landau, where she will continue working on the Shield of the Americas initiative. On Friday, Noem shared a screenshot of a comment from the Department of State regarding her change in position. "The Special Envoy to the Shield of the Americas role was always a six-month appointment," the statement said. "Secretary Noem remains at the State Department as a Senior Advisor." Noem Shares Photo of Dog, Gun on Opening Day of Pheasant Season On Saturday, social media expressed concern over the dog pictured with Noem in her X post. "Happy Opener, South Dakota! Foster and I wish you good luck in the field! Pheasant hunting is part of who we are, and it’s a tradition worth passing on to our kids and grandkids," Noem wrote in the post. "As Governor, I partnered with landowners to start the Second Century Initiative, helping turn marginal land into wildlife habitat so the next generation can enjoy the same hunting traditions we grew up with." In the photo included with the post, Noem is seen wearing hunting gear, holding a rifle, and posing with a dog that looks to be a Vizsla. The post, which has received 2.2 million views as of Saturday afternoon, prompted thousands of comments. Many of them expressed concern over the dog's wellbeing. "Save the dog," one user posted. "Please don't kill him," another commented. "The worst possible thing you could post would be a dog and a gun, lady. Come on," a third wrote. The same post on Facebook prompted similar comments. Pheasant hunting season in South Dakota begins on October 17 and ends on January 31. Dogs play an important role in the activity, as they can locate where the birds are hiding and then signal to their owners. Dogs can also charge at the bird, forcing it to fly into the air and giving the hunter a chance to shoot. Kristi Noem Dog Controversy Explained The excerpts from Noem's biography No Going Back: The Truth on What's Wrong with Politics and How We Move America Forward were published by British newspaper The Guardian in April 2024. In one part, Noem described shooting Cricket after it attacked a family's chickens and tried to bite Noem when she tried to grab the dog. In addition to saying Cricket was "untrainable," Noem wrote that she "hated that dog." Later, Noem defended her actions in an interview with Fox News, saying she killed Cricket because she was concerned for the safety of her children. "You know, that story was a choice as a mom. The safety of my children versus a dangerous dog that was killing livestock and attacking people," she said at the time. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Noem posted the photo a day after news broke that she was no longer special envoy to the Shield of the Americas.

news.title: California Dems don’t care about your safety — that’s why they’ve opposed the border wall
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s border wall still isn’t finished, and won’t be until late 2027, at the earliest. But don’t blame him for that. 

Blame California Democrats and left-wing groups that have tried to stop it.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin reminded America this week that one of the reasons the wall took so long was because of opposition by Gavin Newsom, among others.

The “wall” was the signature promise of Trump’s first term. Democrats knew that if he built that wall, he would be seen as a successful president — and not just as a fluke.

So they were determined to prevent him from building it. And California Democrats led the way. 

In Congress, San Francisco’s Nancy Pelosi refused to fund the wall — even though many Democrats had voted to reinforce fencing along the border just a few years before.

Pelosi and her partner in obstruction from New York, Chuck Schumer, shut down the government rather than fund the wall.

In the end, Trump relented — but used emergency funds to start construction.

Democrats — and a host of interest groups — sued to stop him.

The state of California was among the litigants. They fought Trump in court, slowing down construction — until, under President Joe Biden, the federal government settled.

By then, Biden had already abandoned billions of dollars in construction equipment to rust in the desert sun, next to the unfinished wall.

But Democrats were proud. California Attorney General Rob Bonta took credit for leading 18 other states in legal action against the border wall.

“The Trump Border Wall is officially a relic of the past, which is where it belongs,” Bonta said.

Meanwhile, millions of illegal migrants were pouring into the country.

A year later, voters put Trump back in the White House. And today, illegal border crossings are down to near-zero.

And the wall is being built. No longer a “relic of history,” the wall is part of a successful system of border security. 

When it is completed, the entire country will benefit. Even Democrats.

Democrats may not want to admit it, but border security is an absolute must before immigration reform. 

The public will not support amnesty for those already here, unless we can be sure no more migrants will follow.

Newsom might know that. Maybe that’s why, of the 100 lawsuits California has filed against Trump in his second term, a border wall challenge isn’t one of them.

news.title: Trump biographer singles out the next 'inevitable' White House firing
news.text:
President Donald Trump's White House is once again embroiled in chaos after the abrupt departure of his new press secretary, and now, his one-time biographer has predicted the "inevitable" next firing from the administration.

Within the span of a work week, right-wing commentator Katie Zacharia made her debut as White House press secretary in a disastrously bad briefing, was caught out for false claims about being a lawyer and was pushed out of the office after just five days. news.title: Democrats’ ‘debanking’ abuses show they’re the big threat to democracy
news.text:
With Democrats poised to regain much of their Washington muscle, it’s ever more urgent to notice how they abused that power so recently.

Consider Wednesday’s blockbuster report from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency outlining how nine big banks, including JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, used purely political criteria to deny services to perfectly lawful consumers — when getting “debanked” is often a financial death sentence.

And the debankers regularly relied on the hatemongering-for-profit Southern Poverty Law Center as an authority for who to ban.

This was no small abuse: The OCC investigation covered more than 100,000 consumer complaints and 50,000 internal bank documents.

A JPMorgan payment platform booted merchants with “MAGA” and “America First” in their profiles — and another for working with a group whose “crime” was that a member accurately described the Black Lives Matter movement as Marxist. 

PNC refused a credit line to an outfit that, per the bank’s internal docs, “funded several Christian conservative groups, including several identified as hate groups by the Southern Poverty Law Center” and whose owner was “a conservative political commentator.” 

Yes, this largely happened under President Joe Biden and subsided once he was gone — but the push for it started long before.

In 2019, for example, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez publicly argued, “Not everything has to be done through legislation explicitly” of her and her party’s own efforts to stop banks working with “evil” industries like firearms and oil and gas.

And banks followed those political signals.

Wells Fargo declined to lend money to two firearms businesses; BofA axed private-prison businesses over “changing policymaker attitudes.”

The woke crusade against disfavored industries and speech was, of course, always going to end with average Americans getting punished for lawful behavior. 

It also ended up hurting leftists as well: Capital One refused to bank a group devoted to “reproductive rights [that was] synonymous with abortion and the Dems.” 

These OCC findings are an ugly echo of recent revelations from the Senate Judiciary Committee that special prosecutor Jack Smith, in his Ahab-like pursuit of President Donald Trump, illegally surveilled thousands of Americans for the crime of donating tiny amounts to the president’s campaign. 

The nine banks the OCC report names promise not to abuse again; that’s far from sufficient. If the OCC doesn’t take action, the Consumer Financial Protection Board should exercise its broad enforcement powers here to permanently make debanking efforts expensive and risk-laden for anyone engaging in them.

Don’t leave the door open for Woke 2 Democrats to outdo the “craaazy” Woke 1 crew: Just imagine the financial sanctions against people who object to gender extremism, criticize Hamas, don’t want open borders or support locking up criminals. 

Democrats show no shame or regret over the OCC findings, making it plain that the extremists still call the shots — and will stay in the driver’s seat for the foreseeable future.

Unless and until the normies reclaim their party, every Democratic victory adds a new threat to our democracy.

news.title: Veteran Hollywood actress shreds Nithya Raman over remarks about ex-police chief: ‘Where is your apology?’
news.text:
A Hollywood actress and ally of LA Mayor Karen Bass is demanding an apology from mayoral challenger Nithya Raman over comments praising a controversial policy from disgraced former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates, calling the remarks a “historical error” and a “personal assault.”

Anne-Marie Johnson, best known for her roles in Hill Street Blues and Double Trouble, blasted the socialist city councilmember at a Thursday event hosted by Bass.

“Nithya, where’s the apology?” she said loudly, while looking straight at the camera. “We’re running out of time. We need an apology.”

The fiery rebuke comes after Raman criticized Bass during a mayoral debate this week over reports that LAPD shared information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement — a flashpoint for liberal Angelenos opposed to President Donald Trump’s deportation crackdown.

Raman argued that Los Angeles had abandoned its historic resistance to federal immigration enforcement, invoking Gates’ tenure as police chief.

“This city used to be the gold standard in terms of non-cooperation with immigration enforcement, years ago under the era of Daryl Gates,” the socialist city councilmember said at the debate.

“And now under this mayor, we’ve actually lost trust from our immigrant community in our city and in our law enforcement.”

Bass has seized on the remarks, accusing her challenger of overlooking the city’s painful history of police abuse, particularly against Black and Latino residents during Gates’ tenure.

“My opponent is not really familiar with L.A., especially the Black community,” Bass said. “She doesn’t know us.”

Gates became a symbol of police brutality during his time leading the LAPD, which was rocked by the 1991 beating of Black motorist Rodney King. The officers’ acquittals in 1992 helped ignite the city’s devastating riots.

Johnson said the debate remarks hit close to home. Her father served as a police officer alongside Gates, and she lives in Raman’s City Council district.

“I think I’m the only African American she sees,” she remarked snidely. 

Johnson then invoked one of Gates’ most notorious comments: his suggestion that Black men might die more frequently from police chokeholds because their veins or arteries did not open up as quickly as those of “normal people.”

“Gold standard there, Daryl Gates,” Johnson added, referencing Raman’s comment. 

“This is what ignorance brings to us. This is what a limited education from social media brings to us. I’d like to drop off an encyclopedia to her door step so she understands the power and the pain and the domestic terrorism we all had to live through during the Daryl Gates reign,” Johnson said, before repeating her demand for an apology.

The actress recalled how hard it was for her family, one of the very few black families around, to try to move into the Silver Lake neighborhood that’s currently in Raman’s district.

“This is all very personal to me,” Johnson said.

Raman has pushed back against Bass’ criticism, posting a video in which she called Gates “an abhorrent and racist police chief” and insisted she was referring specifically to his Special Order 40.

The policy was designed to reassure immigrants that they could report crimes or serve as witnesses without fearing deportation, though it did not prohibit LAPD cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

“Over and over, I have challenged Mayor Bass over reports of LAPD cooperation with ICE under her leadership,” Raman said in a statement. “Now Mayor Bass is deliberately twisting my words to distract from the questions she is refusing to answer.”

Gates resigned in 1992 amid mounting criticism of police abuse, with the Rodney King beating becoming a defining scandal of his tenure.
news.summary: "This is all very personal to me," she said.
news.author: Titus Wu

news.title: GOP Whip Calls For Squad's Ilhan Omar to Be "Jailed and Deported" If Her Citizenship Is a Lie
news.text:
Tom Emmer, the number three Republican in the House and highest-ranking lawmaker from Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-MN) home state, is calling for the Somalia-born leftist to be jailed and deported if it is found she or her family lied on her citizenship paperwork.

Omar is under federal investigation as the result of allegations that reportedly include she and/or her father lied about when she was born on immigration paperwork in order to obtain her citizenship after her family fled the troubled African country in the 1990s.

If her reported birthdate indicating she was younger than 18 at the time of her naturalization was false, her citizenship would not be valid and she would not qualify for the naturalization requirement for her to serve in Congress.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-MN) told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that “there have been rumors for years” about Omar.

“If proven true, she should face consequences,” he said.

Omar and other Democrats, including House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, (D-NY) have been pushing back, claiming the probe is a political persecution by President Donald Trump against a lawmaker who is a frequent critic.

They also accuse the administration of malevolent timing with the investigation surfacing weeks before the critical midterm election.

But Emmer didn’t hold back.

He told Fox, “I would say first she should probably serve time in the gray bar motel and then get the hell out of here. She should go back to where she came from … [i]f it’s determined that she lied to gain citizenship.”

Omar is a member of the high-profile, far-left legislative clique known as the “Squad” with other members, including Reps. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY).

Earlier this week federal agents raided Omar’s home and seized her cellphone as well as other items.

The allegations are reportedly linked to her father becoming an American citizen in 2000, the year supporters say Omar was 17, automatically qualifying her for naturalized citizenship as a legal minor and daughter of a naturalized citizen.

If she was 18, as recently alleged by some, she would have to seek citizenship through the established process herself for those immigrants, such as green card holders, who seek it.

Omar posted on X after the raid:

I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.

Omar’s allies and other critics of the probe have called it an unprecedented action with fewer than three weeks before midterm Election Day on Nov. 3.

Jeffries and his top deputies called the raid “deeply disturbing” and essentially accused the president of immigration lawfare.

Emmer countered bluntly.

“I think she is a liar,” Emmer told Fox on camera. “I think she is a fraud.”

Emmer argued the probe was not political, pointing to the judicially authorized search warrant for Omar’s home.

“That judge had to determine that there was probable cause that a federal crime has been committed,” Emmer said. “And I’ll tell you what, as long as it was Ilhan Omar, it was going to be scrutinized to the very detail.”

He added, “So the fact that they issued the warrant in the first place and then executed it, I mean maybe after all these years, someone is finally going to hold Ilhan Omar accountable.”
